The structure of these courses tends towards an excessive verbosity, which is so pervasive that the entirety of the content could be feasibly condensed into an 8-hour delivery without sacrificing the necessary concepts. Such verbosity serves as a roadblock to effective learning; essential details become hard to absorb and sometimes disappear in the deluge of extraneous information.

Counter-arguments may be raised based on the below-average grades in final exams, suggesting that perhaps verbosity isn't the issue. However, this perspective misses the mark. The problem, in fact, lies within the verbosity itself. Students often struggle to glean the essential principles from the information overload, remembering less critical details, and frequently forgetting the foundational concepts. As a result, their grades suffer.

Addressing this issue at an institutional level may be challenging, but as individuals, learners can adopt more efficient strategies to circumnavigate the verbosity. It can be beneficial to begin with shorter videos that encapsulate key concepts without overwhelming the learner with unnecessary details. Once grasped, they can then venture into the more verbose content, allowing for the refining and consolidation of smaller, yet crucial, details within a manageable scope of information. In this way, learners can strategically reduce the detrimental effects of verbosity, ultimately leading to improved academic performance.

Microwave Electronics is a must for everyone who is interested in RF and EM in general. The course is not math or derivation-intensive, and the subjects are more design-oriented. It closely resembles EEE313 Electronic Circuit Design in its structure and pacing. The course has lab sessions, homework assignments, and a not-so-easy project. All of these require consistent effort throughout the semester.

The strongest aspect of the course has to be the project. You design and simulate a microwave circuit from scratch using ADS, draw a suitable PCB layout, which is then manufactured. You get to solder SMD components whose size rivals the thickness of human hair :) . You also learn how to operate industry-standard RF equipment such as vector network analyzers, spectrum analyzers, noise meters, etc., all of which are used to test the final project.

Having hands-on experience to this extent is very rare in undergraduate courses (not just at Bilkent), and it requires a certain level of involvement from the student. If you are not interested in RF, do not take this course, otherwise all of this will feel like a chore. Also, try not to take too many EE courses along with EEE412, it has enough workload to keep you busy.
